officialDocs.label: Guidelines for responsible use of Automattic's APIs

verdict.summary: Registering an OAuth app is self-serve with no review or approval step described, API use is free, and any WordPress.com user (including Jetpack-connected self-hosted sites, with a global token) can authorize the same day. The main decisions are per-blog vs. 'global' tokens, and the classic /oauth2 endpoints vs. the newer OAuth 2.1 endpoints (PKCE, refresh tokens) advertised in WordPress.com's discovery document.

evidence.label: inferred
evidence.note: Create an app at developer.wordpress.com/apps/new, copy the client ID and secret, and run the code flow. There's no review.

timeToProd.assumes: An agent that reads or writes posts, media, comments or stats on users' WordPress.com or Jetpack sites via REST API tokens.

evidence.label: inferred
evidence.note: Neither the OAuth2 docs nor the API guidelines describe an app approval process. Automattic can terminate access at its discretion.

prerequisites.why: Apps are created in the Applications manager, which redirects to WordPress.com login.

prerequisites.item: An HTTPS redirect URI that matches exactly
prerequisites.why: All OAuth2 communication has to use HTTPS, and redirect_uri has to match the registered URI exactly (even a trailing slash matters).

evidence.label: sourced
evidence.note: The docs don't address http://localhost for development.

prerequisites.item: A decision on per-blog vs. global access
prerequisites.why: Default tokens cover one blog. The global scope covers all of the user's WordPress.com sites and connected Jetpack sites.

scopeTiers.impact: auth limits the token to the /me endpoint. The OAuth 2.1 discovery document also advertises OIDC scopes and a userinfo endpoint.

evidence.label: tested
evidence.note: OIDC scopes observed in the live discovery document.

scopeTiers.impact: The token is bound to one blog (blog_id and blog_url are returned with it). Good for an agent that drafts posts or moderates comments on one site.
Access to all of the user's WordPress.com sites and connected Jetpack sites. The docs advise requesting it only when truly needed, but no approval is described.

steps.title: Sign in and create an application
steps.detail: In the Applications manager, create a new app with name, description, website, redirect URL(s) and type. Copy the Client ID and Client Secret.

evidence.label: sourced
evidence.note: Form fields beyond the redirect URI weren't observed because we didn't sign in.

steps.title: Choose classic OAuth2 or the OAuth 2.1 endpoints
steps.detail: Classic: https://public-api.wordpress.com/oauth2/authorize and /oauth2/token, documented in the OAuth2 guide. OAuth 2.1: /oauth2-1/authorize, /oauth2-1/token, /oauth2-1/revoke, with PKCE S256, refresh_token grants and dynamic client registration, advertised in the discovery document and used by the MCP server.

evidence.label: tested
evidence.note: The discovery document was observed on 2026-10-20. We found no developer guide for using /oauth2-1 with your own registered app, so treat that path as less documented.

steps.title: Pick least-privilege scopes
steps.detail: Default to a single-blog token with only the scopes needed (for example, posts and media). Use global only if the agent truly works across many sites.

steps.title: Implement the authorization code flow
steps.detail: Redirect to https://public-api.wordpress.com/oauth2/authorize?client_id=...&redirect_uri=...&response_type=code&scope=...&state=... (optionally blog=<id or URL>). POST the code to /oauth2/token with client_id, client_secret, redirect_uri, code and grant_type=authorization_code. Store access_token with blog_id/blog_url.

steps.title: Validate tokens and handle expiry
steps.detail: Use GET /oauth2/token-info?client_id=...&token=... to confirm user, blog and scope. Implicit tokens are documented to expire after two weeks, and code-flow expiry isn't documented, so treat a 401 as 'reconnect' (or use the 2.1 refresh_token grant).

steps.title: Test against WordPress.com and Jetpack sites
steps.detail: Authorize with a second account that owns a WordPress.com site and, if relevant, a Jetpack-connected self-hosted site. Confirm the consent screen and API calls work for both.

evidence.label: sourced
evidence.note: The docs say the endpoints work consistently for WordPress.com and Jetpack-connected sites.

steps.title: Review the API usage guidelines
steps.detail: Check the product against Automattic's terms: no excessive calls, refresh cached data at reasonable intervals, never store user passwords, don't use 'WordPress'/'Automattic' branding without consent, and don't use user data to market competing products.

steps.title: Launch
steps.detail: Switch to production redirect URIs. No submission or review is described, so any WordPress.com user can connect.

Implement the code flow, token-info checks and reconnects
Probe the discovery document and token endpoints
Check the product against Automattic's API guidelines
humanMustDo: Sign in to WordPress.com and create the app
Test with real WordPress.com and Jetpack sites

blockers.symptom: Authorization fails with a redirect_uri mismatch
blockers.cause: The redirect_uri differs from the registered URI, even by a trailing slash.
blockers.fix: Register and send the exact same URI.

blockers.cause: The token request is missing client credentials.
blockers.fix: POST client_id, client_secret, code, redirect_uri and grant_type as form fields.

blockers.symptom: The agent can only see one of the user's sites
blockers.fix: Request the global scope if you need all sites, or run one authorization per blog.

blockers.symptom: API calls start returning 401 after a while
blockers.cause: The token expired (implicit tokens after two weeks) or the user revoked access.
blockers.fix: Prefer the code flow, check tokens with token-info, and send the user through consent again, or use the OAuth 2.1 refresh grant.

blockers.symptom: Password grant works locally but not for customers
blockers.cause: The password grant only works with your own credentials and is for development only.
blockers.fix: Use the authorization code flow in production. With 2FA on, use an Application Password for local testing.

nuances.text: The classic docs describe no refresh tokens and conflict on lifetime (implicit tokens 'expire after two weeks', but the example shows expires_in=64800). The OAuth 2.1 discovery document does list a refresh_token grant.
No numeric rate limits are published. Automattic only prohibits 'excessive API calls' as it determines in its sole discretion.
API use is free, and stored WordPress.com data has to be refreshed at reasonable intervals. Automattic can end access at any time with or without cause.

WordPress.com runs its own MCP server (OAuth 2.1 with PKCE and dynamic client registration) on paid plans, free sites for their first 30 days, and Jetpack AI/Complete. Users may connect AI clients directly without your app.
The API guidelines say nothing about AI/ML use. The restriction that does apply is not using user information to market products that compete with Automattic.
